work_order.confidence_rationale: Every defect in this order was reproduced from scratch in my own sandbox against a real git remote, and every fix was applied there and re-measured — including the latin1 change's own regression risk (a valid UTF-8 filename), and the C fixture's falsifiability by removing the 'C' arm and watching that one case fail. The AC-8 regression comparison and the AC-10 catch were run across every branch. Held below 90 by four things I could not run in this checkout: there is no node_modules, so I could not run yarn typecheck, yarn lint, or the package's own vitest run (I executed the parser directly against stubbed gray-matter/listify instead, which covers the C fixture but not the full suite as the runner will execute it); I ran on Node 22 while CI pins Node 24; and no live Actions run was observed. The typecheck surface is also worth a second look — the root tsconfig sets allowJs with checkJs false, so the Buffer flowing through bin/*.mjs is unlikely to be typechecked at all, but I did not run the compiler to confirm.
work_order.understanding:
PR #30 hardened the release-notes gate's reporting path but left several of its assumptions about the environment standing, and the parser kept an untested branch. I re-reproduced every finding independently in a clean sandbox (/tmp/arb33, bare remote, real `git fetch origin baseRef` + `git diff origin/base...HEAD`) against the current script on main, applied the proposed fixes there, and measured the before/after myself.

CRASHES — an uncaught throw where a ::error:: line belongs. (1) Line 20's module-level `fs.realpathSync(NOTES_DIR)` runs before any error handling: `git rm -r upcoming-release-notes` dies at module evaluation with `Error: ENOENT ... lstat`, exit 1, zero ::error:: lines. Two reviewers filed this as separate findings; it is one defect. (2) `fs.createWriteStream(GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY)` registers only a `close` listener, so an unopenable summary path kills the process with `Unhandled 'error' event`. Its two sibling calls were guarded in #30; this one was not.

SILENT TRUNCATION. (3) `process.exit(1)` immediately after a `console.log` that can emit the whole README (a PR author controls those bytes). `process.stdout` to a pipe is async, so the write is discarded mid-flight. I measured 65688 bytes against a 200113-byte README, and 65586 against a 160128-byte ::error:: line — both cut at the 64KB pipe buffer. The same root cause truncates the ::error:: line itself, so QA's separate truncation report is not a separate bug.

FALSE REJECTION. (4) `promisify(execFile)` decodes git's stdout as UTF-8, discarding the byte fidelity `-z` buys one step later. I confirmed with a hexdump that git emits the raw byte `6e e9 2d` in the path field; UTF-8 decoding turns it into U+FFFD, so `fs.existsSync` misses a file that is genuinely there and the gate reports 'was added but does not exist on HEAD'.

UNTESTED BRANCH. (5) The C arm's only fixture was deleted in #30. I confirmed unreachability by running git rather than reasoning: under the production invocation a byte-identical copy arrives as `A`, and adding `--find-copies-harder` drops the row entirely at `--diff-filter=AMR` — unreachable for two independent mechanisms. The reviewer pre-blessed keeping the literal C, so this is coverage, not behaviour.

FIFTH DEFECT — found by me, in neither the ticket nor the proposal. `await execFile('git', ['fetch', 'origin', baseRef])` at line 107 is the first statement of an async IIFE with no `.catch`. If the fetch fails (base branch deleted or renamed, transient network), the rejection is unhandled and the gate dies with a raw `Error: Command failed: git fetch origin ...` stack trace and zero ::error:: lines — the exact contract violation the other four findings are about. A branch deleted out from under an open PR is ordinary, not exotic. I added it here because it is the same class in the same function and I verified the fix is non-regressive; it is disclosed rather than folded in silently.

The PR title finding is a `gh pr edit` on an already-merged PR, not a code change; recorded in out_of_scope with the exact command rather than dropped.
work_order.root_cause: Three assumptions, all in the gate's reporting path rather than its validation logic. (a) It treats its environment as guaranteed — the presence of `upcoming-release-notes/`, of `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`'s parent directory, and of a reachable base ref — so ordinary situations reach I/O that throws instead of reporting; #30 fixed two such calls inside reportError and left the other three. (b) It treats `process.exit` as a way to finish writing: on a pipe `console.log` is asynchronous, so exiting synchronously discards whatever had not drained, which is why the truncation scales with how much a PR author controls. (c) It reads git's stdout through a UTF-8 decoder that cannot represent every byte a POSIX filename may hold, throwing away the byte-exactness `-z` was adopted for.
work_order.approach:
Five changes to release-notes-check.mjs, one fixture to util.test.js, plus a release note.

(1) Delete the module-level `realpathSync` line outright rather than guarding it — it is debug output nothing reads (`grep -rn 'Looking in'` finds no other reference) and every message already names the directory. A deleted directory then reaches `git diff`, reports the deletions, and takes the normal reportError path.

(2) Wrap the `git fetch` in try/catch inside the async IIFE, routing a failure to `reportError` and returning. This is the same 'report an error rather than throw one' contract reportError already states for its own reads.

(3) Replace both `process.exit(1)` calls in reportError with `process.exitCode = 1` and `return`, so the process ends naturally once stdout drains — the same async path the summary-set branch already used, making the branches consistent rather than adding a third exit style.

(4) Attach an `error` listener to the summary stream alongside `close`, both setting exitCode, and call `summary.end(readme)` last so the listener is registered before the open is attempted. The verdict is already on stdout; only the unhandled event kills the process.

(5) Ask git for latin1 rather than UTF-8 and rebuild each path with `Buffer.from(name, 'latin1')` before it reaches the filesystem. latin1 is byte-preserving, so it is an exact inverse (I verified the round trip is byte-identical), and `path.toString('utf-8')` recovers the display string so valid UTF-8 names still print correctly — confirmed with `café.md`, which validates and whose error message shows no replacement characters. `validateFile` takes the display label as a second argument; note there are **seven** reportError calls in it, not six — grep for them rather than trusting a count.

`selectReleaseNotePaths` is untouched apart from the added fixture: its filters are ASCII (`endsWith('.md')`, the README comparison) and its status column is ASCII, so all are already correct on a latin1 view. Changing its signature would churn 32 tests for no behavioural gain, as would touching SELECTED_STATUSES or the diff filter — both pre-blessed and verified correct.

The new C fixture is falsifiable, not decorative: I removed the `'C'` from `hasTwoPaths` and confirmed the new case fails while the rest pass, then restored it.

risks: The latin1 decode is the one change reaching past a crash fix into a semantic choice. A future caller of selectReleaseNotePaths passing genuinely UTF-8 strings rather than the latin1 view this gate produces would double-encode its paths. The comment at the loop must explain the invariant; there is no other production caller today (grep confirms release-notes-check.mjs:123 and util.test.js are the only two), but the contract is inherited silently.

Changing process.exit(1) to process.exitCode = 1 relies on nothing else keeping the event loop alive on those paths. True today (reportError returns; on the summary path the stream keeps the loop alive until close, which is what the old code waited for), but a future edit leaving a pending handle on the unset-summary path would hang instead of exit — worse than truncation, though harder rather than easier to introduce.
Deleting the 'Looking in' line removes the only absolute path the gate prints; anyone debugging a checkout-symlink or case-sensitivity problem from the job log loses that hint.

The C fixture encodes today's git behaviour as a passing test but feeds the parser a synthetic row rather than running git — it proves the consumption logic, not the invocation's reachability, which is what the reviewer asked for but worth stating plainly.

The fetch-failure catch is an addition beyond the nine items in the ticket. It is the same defect class in the same function and I verified it changes no other branch's output, but it is not something the issue asked for and a reviewer may reasonably ask why it is here.

work_order.debate_summary:
The critique is empty — plan/critique.json is `{}`, so there was nothing to judge. Per the arbiter spec I did not treat that as a reason to stop; I re-derived the proposal's claims against the code and reproduced all of them myself, then ruled on the proposal alone. Every load-bearing claim held up: the ENOENT crash at line 20, the unhandled stream error, the 64KB truncation (I measured 65688 and 65586 against 200113 and 160128 fixed), the false rejection of a 0xE9 filename (confirmed with a hexdump of git's own output that the raw byte survives), and the C arm's double unreachability. I found no unfounded claim to dismiss, but I did find two places where the proposal is wrong in its details.

First, the proposal tells the implementer to thread a display label through validateFile's 'six reportError calls'. There are seven. Small, but it is a literal instruction an implementer could follow by counting and would silently leave one message printing a Buffer. I corrected it and told the implementer to grep.

Second, and more substantively: the proposal's AC-8 claims the regression branches produce byte-identical output to the unmodified script. They do not — deleting the 'Looking in' line changes every one of them. That is the intended consequence of a fix the proposal itself argues for, so this is a wording defect rather than a wrong plan, but an acceptance criterion that cannot pass as written is worse than none, since it would send QA looking for a behaviour change that was never intended. I restated it as 'identical apart from the removed debug line', which is what I actually measured.

Where I departed from both the ticket and the proposal: I added a fifth defect neither mentions. Line 107's `git fetch` sits at the top of an async IIFE with no `.catch`, so an unfetchable base ref — a deleted branch, a rename, a transient network failure — kills the gate with an unhandled rejection and a raw `Error: Command failed` stack, zero ::error:: lines. I verified this crashes today and that wrapping it in try/catch routing to reportError produces a proper ::error:: at exit 1, with no other branch's output changing. I included it because it is the same defect class in the same function as the four the ticket is about, and because leaving a known crash of exactly the kind this ticket exists to remove seemed worse than a disclosed addition. It is listed in risks so a reviewer can strike it if they disagree; nothing else in the work depends on it.

Two smaller judgements. The ticket says 'Split this if they were unrelated' — they are not; all nine items are the same three assumptions in one 143-line file, and one root-cause fix covers them. And the ticket's QA entries were written against PR #30 as it stood; I re-ran all four rather than trusting them, and all four still reproduce on current main. Note that the two reviewer findings about line 20 are one defect, not two, despite being filed separately — the ticket's title counts them as distinct.

No decisions in plan/brief.md contradict anything here; the brief records nothing, and the issue has no '## Acceptance (from the split)' section, so there are no IAC-n obligations to satisfy or defer.
residual_risks: No checked-in test covers the five bin/ fixes; they are verified only by the qa_script, run by hand. The crash and truncation classes are exactly the kind that regress silently — a future module-scope fs call, a fetch without a catch, or process.exitCode swapped back for process.exit, passes every test in the repo. Moving reportError into src/ to make it unit-testable is the real fix and a larger refactor than these findings justify.

The 200KB-README and 20000-author truncation scenarios need a deliberately pathological PR and will not occur naturally in review, so a regression there would not be caught until someone constructed one.

If GitHub normalises non-UTF-8 paths on checkout, the AC-5 scenario may be unreachable through Actions and only exercised locally — the fix is still correct, but AC-5 could be quietly skipped as unreproducible in CI.
The 64KB figure is what a pipe buffer gives on this platform; the threshold is environment-dependent, so QA should compare against the pre-change number on the same machine rather than against 65536.

Nothing here changes which notes the gate selects or how it judges them — SELECTED_STATUSES, the diff filter and every validation rule are untouched. A reviewer skimming may read the latin1 line as a behaviour change to path selection; it is not, and AC-8 is the check for that.

The fetch-failure message embeds git's own stderr, which is sanitized for workflow-command syntax but is otherwise passed through. That matches how every other reportError message is built, but it does mean a base-ref name chosen by a PR author appears in the log.

latin1 round-trips exactly for any byte a POSIX filename may hold. Verified for 0xE9 (invalid UTF-8) and café.md (valid UTF-8), where both the lookup and the printed message are correct; I did not enumerate every byte value.

Whether the ~200KB README scenario is reachable through GitHub. Actions has its own step-summary and log size limits I did not look up; the truncation I fixed is in the gate's own stdout before those apply.
How often an unfetchable base ref occurs in practice on this repo's Actions setup. I verified the crash and the fix in a sandbox, not from a real failed fetch in a real run.

risks: Adding the boundary means a programming error inside the gate now reads as 'Release notes check failed: ...' rather than as a crash. That is the deliberate trade this whole ticket asks for — the same one reportError already made for its reads — but it means a future bug in the gate can be mistaken for a contributor's mistake. The message carries the real error text, which is what makes that recoverable; do not also dump a stack to stderr, because several criteria check stderr is empty.

parseNote now returns a tagged result rather than throwing, so validateFile's first lines change shape. Every one of its seven reportError messages must keep its exact current text or AC-8's byte-for-byte comparison fails. Grep for them rather than trusting the count.

The 64MB maxBuffer is a magic number with a comment. A pathological diff now costs up to 64MB of resident buffer before it errors, which is a deliberate exchange: an error that names itself is cheaper than a process that dies.

The two spawned-gate cases run real git. They create a bare remote and commit under a tmpdir on every suite run — fast, but they are the first tests in this package to shell out, so they can fail on a machine with no git identity or an unusual git default branch name.
